content_metadata.description: This video provides an alternative method of rigging the DD XL tarp, focusing on flexibility and adaptability for various weather conditions.

qAndA.answer: He does not attach the tarp to the ridgeline. Instead, he rotates the tarp 180 degrees and uses the tie-outs at the ends (originally the middle) to connect to foliage.
qAndA.question: How does the narrator attach the tarp to the ridgeline in his alternative method?

qAndA.answer: He prefers this setup because it allows him to easily unclip the front section of the tarp and reposition it to change the tarp's dynamics based on weather conditions and the number of hammocks or items he's covering.
qAndA.question: Why does the narrator prefer having the ridgeline running underneath the tarp?

qAndA.answer: He mentions that hanging the tarp in this way allows him to pack it away using only one skin.
qAndA.question: What specific advantage does the narrator highlight about his method in terms of packing?

qAndA.answer: He suggests using walking poles to prop up the tarp and create a porch.
qAndA.question: What item does the narrator suggest using in good weather to create a porch area?

youtube_description:
I recently discovered that if you take the DD XL tarp and suspend it with the ridge-line underneath, then rotate the tarp by 180 degrees and clip it to the ridge-line, using what used to be the centre tie-outs from each side, this affords a number of benefits:

1) If like me, you store it in a snakeskin; you now only need one skin instead of two.
2) You can use the loops that run along the top of the old ridge-line axis as side tie-outs, which make it more spacious and less prone to sagging in heavy rain.
3) Even in a standard A-frame set-up, the porch area you can create in nice weather - by tying off to foliage or pegging out via hiking poles, is much bigger.
4) In bad weather, using the A-frame set up, you can now easily create doors by clipping the centre tie-outs from each short side together and re-pegging.
5) Before you peg it out, you can easily move the tarp over by one loop, allowing an even greater porch area or the ability to cover more than one hammock.

I forgot to mention it in the video but I'm using tendertoe1's method of suspending from the ridgeline: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ktNuOa6PSZI
